query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior of HfNbTaTiZr stems from residual internal stresses generated by thermal expansion mismatch during solidification and processing. These mismatched expansion strains create heterogeneous stress fields that alter dislocation formation and motion as well as modify the effective elastic moduli, thereby unifying observations from cold rolling, aging-induced hardening, elastic modulus temperature dependence, and high‐temperature creep.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy produced by conventional casting/solidification and then processed by cold rolling and aging (i.e., exhibiting a composite-like microstructure with inherent thermal expansion mismatch induced residual stresses).
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) a control group processed under standard conditions (retaining thermal mismatch induced residual stresses) and (b) a comparison group that undergoes an extended isothermal annealing treatment designed to relax residual thermal stresses without significantly altering the phase or grain structure.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing and thermal analysis carried out over a wide temperature range – with elastic modulus measured from 293 K to 1100 K, and tensile creep tests around 1250 °C; cold rolling and aging treatments (600–800 °C) are considered within processing boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Residual heterogeneous stresses (and associated dislocation/defect networks) generated by differential thermal expansion during composite solidification and post-casting processing.
generation.mechanism: During solidification (or composite solidification), different regions develop due to variations in thermal contraction. This induces residual stresses that bias the nucleation and evolution of dislocation networks and lattice distortions. These internal stresses then enhance work hardening during cold rolling, adjust elastic moduli with temperature, and modify the activation energy for dislocation creep at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples retaining the residual thermal stresses will exhibit: (1) enhanced microhardness after cold rolling; (2) a more pronounced temperature dependence in elastic moduli from 293 K to 1100 K; and (3) improved creep resistance at ~1250 °C compared to stress-relaxed samples. In contrast, annealed (thermal stress-relieved) samples should show a reduced magnitude of these anomalies relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The conventional as-cast and processed HfNbTaTiZr alloy with inherent thermal mismatch induced residual stresses.
generation.boundary: Temperature response is examined from room temperature (293 K) up to the elastic testing limit (1100 K) and under high-temperature creep conditions at ~1250 °C. Processing boundaries include cold rolling and aging treatments (600–800 °C) that contribute to microstructural evolution.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent to which the thermal expansion mismatch contributes relative to other factors (e.g., intrinsic lattice distortion or compositional heterogeneity) is not fully established, and further studies are needed to isolate its relative impact.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one processed by standard methods (retaining residual thermal stresses) and one subjected to prolonged isothermal annealing at a moderate temperature to relieve these residual stresses. Then perform in situ mechanical tests (elastic modulus measurements over 293–1100 K and tensile creep tests at ~1250 °C) as well as microstructural residual stress mapping (via XRD or in situ neutron diffraction).
measurements: Microhardness after cold rolling and aging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If relaxation of the residual stresses (as evidenced by stress mapping) does not lead to a corresponding reduction or significant change in the elastic modulus temperature dependence, high-temperature creep resistance, or cold-rolling-induced microhardness, then the hypothesis linking these behaviors to thermal expansion mismatch is falsified.

Temperature dependence of elastic and plastic deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy

Abstract: The present work discovers the unique deformation behavior of a refractory high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures. Single-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show remarkable mechanical properties, such as their high yield strength and substantial softening resistance at elevated temperatures. Hence, the in-depth study of the deformation behavior for body-centered cubic (BCC) refractory HEAs is a critical issue to explore the uncovered/unique deformation mechanisms. We have investigated the elastic and plastic deformation behaviors of a single BCC NbTaTiV refractory HEA at elevated temperatures using integrated experimental efforts and theoretical calculations. The in situ neutron diffraction results reveal a temperature-dependent elastic anisotropic deformation behavior. The single-crystal elastic moduli and macroscopic Young’s, shear, and bulk moduli were determined from the in situ neutron diffraction, showing great agreement with first-principles calculations, machine learning, and resonant ultrasound spectroscopy results. Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System

Abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.
